This message comes from Kachava. A little boost goes a long way, especially when it comes to caring for your gut during the holiday season and beyond.
Introducing Kachava's new 3-in-1 digestive boost. Simply mix into your favorite Kachava shake or any cold beverage.
Go to kachava.com and use code NPR for 15% off your first order. That's K-A-C-H-A-V-A.com. Code NPR.
Live from NPR News, I'm Charles Snyder. Scott Colombe is Mississippi's Democratic Senator-elect.
For me, this journey started with a prayer, y'all. And in Mississippi, our prayers have often changed the course of history.
Colombe, speaking to supporters in Jackson a short time ago, the Associated Press called his race earlier this evening, more than a week after midterm election day.
Colombe narrowly defeated Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in PR's Elena Moore reports.
This race ultimately came down to just a few thousand votes, taking over a week to call as election officials counted outstanding ballots.
It's a historic Democratic upset and a major blow to Republicans.
Even in a year where Democrats had momentum, the Mississippi Senate race was not expected to be a toss-up heading into election day.
It's long been a ruby red state. Just two years ago, President Trump carried Mississippi by double digits.
Now, Colombe will be the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate in more than 40 years.
He'll also be Mississippi's first black U.S. Senator since Reconstruction.
Elena Moore, NPR News.
A judge has rejected the BBC's request to dismiss President Trump's defamation case. Trump alleges a BBC documentary defamed him by splicing together his remarks before the January 6th Capitol attack.
NPR's David Faucon flick reports.
The BBC argues Trump hadn't alleged any harm.
He withdrew claims of business losses and is seeking to avoid having to share records of his financial holdings and dealings.
And the BBC says the 2024 documentary aired two weeks before the presidential elections wasn't shown in this country, much less Florida, where the case was filed.
That failed to impress the presiding judge, Jeffrey Kuntz, who was appointed by the president and is overseeing the case.
He said the BBC's editing gave the mistaken impression that Trump called for violence.
And the judge said the timing so close to the election bolsters the defamation claim.
Evaluating the case's merits, Judge Kuntz wrote, would fall to another day.
David Faucon flick, NPR News.
A new federal rule requiring Americans and certain immigrants to verify their eligibility could evict tens of thousands of people from public housing, including many U.S. citizen children.
Here's NPR's Jennifer Ludden reporting.
Immigrants in the U.S. unlawfully do not get federal rental aid, but since the 90s, Congress has let them live with family members who do. Housing Secretary Scott Turner calls that exploiting a loophole and says it's not fair to U.S. citizens, especially since rental aid is deeply underfunded and only a quarter of those eligible ever get it.
Housing advocates and other critics say the new rule could separate families and will actually cost more. That's because mixed status households get a smaller subsidy than those where every member is eligible.
In its own analysis, the federal housing agency says that will mean the same budget will help fewer people.
Jennifer Ludden, NPR News, Washington.
And you're listening to NPR News. The board of the influential AI chip maker, NVIDIA, is meeting tonight to decide whether to oust founder and CEO Jensen Huang.
The company is in a leadership crisis after Huang acknowledged an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
President Trump says a triumphal arch he wants to build could also be dedicated to military veterans.
He made that suggestion during his Veterans Day speech at Arlington National Cemetery.
A 250-foot arch would be built nearby, but it's facing legal hurdles. Three veterans have joined a lawsuit to stop the project.
So multiple members of the Kennedy family, they argue the arch would obstruct a clear view of the gray side of former President John F. Kennedy and permanently cast a shadow over the grays of servicemen and women.
No two people have the same fingerprints. NPR's Nate Rott reports on a new study that suggests that may be true of monkeys, too.
The tiny ridges on the surface of your fingers and toes, hands and feet, your fingerprints or footprints, they're called friction ridges, and they're meant to help you grip things.
Their uniqueness has also been used in forensics for humans for a long time, as anyone who watches crime thrillers knows.
This new study, published in the journal PLOS ONE, suggests these ridges could also be used to identify individual primates, too.
Scientists looked at the palm prints and footprints of 116 individual monkeys in Brazil and found that none were the same. More testing, they say, is also needed.
Nate Rott, NPR News.
And I'm Giles Snyder. This is NPR News.
This message comes from Jerry. Many people are overpaying on car insurance. Why? Switching providers can be a pain.
Jerry helps make the process painless. Jerry is the only app that compares rates from over 50 insurers in minutes and helps you switch fast with no spam calls or hidden fees.
